    Reconfigurable hydrogel interfaces for soft brain electrodes

    Zhichang Liu and Sihong Wang https://orcid.org/0000-0002-3611-0004 [redacted-email]Authors Info & Affiliations
    April 20, 2026
    123 (17) e2607267123
    https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2607267123
    Research Article
    March 11, 2026
    A soft electrode array with reconfigurable hydrogel interfaces for high-fidelity neurophysiological monitoring during craniotomy
    Ganguang Yang, Bo Pang [...] Hao Wu
    Track CitationsAdd to Reading List
    PDFEPUB
    Vol. 123 | No. 17
    • Acknowledgments
    • References
    • Information & Authors
    • Metrics & Citations
    • View Options
    • References

    • Tables

    • Share
    Real-time monitoring of neural activity is essential during neurosurgery to minimize unintended damage to healthy brain tissue (1–3). Current approaches typically rely on multichannel electrode arrays placed directly on the brain surface to record electrical signals (4–6). To improve signal quality at this interface, hydrogel layers are often incorporated to promote conformal adhesion between electrodes and the cortical surface (7, 8). However, in the complex biological environment of the brain, these hydrogel interfaces can degrade over time, leading to weakened adhesion and compromised electrical stability (9–11). Writing in PNAS, Yang et al. report a soft electrode array with reconfigurable hydrogel interfaces enabled by a solution-triggered reconfiguration strategy (12). This design allows the hydrogel layer to be repeatedly disassembled and replaced, enabling more reliable and sustained monitoring of electrophysiological signals from the brain surface throughout neurosurgical procedures (Fig. 1A).
    Fig. 1.
    The main innovation in the reconfigurable hydrogel interface design lies in a bilayer hydrogel structure that can be separated on demand. In this bilayer structure, a hydrogel transition layer forms stable covalent bonds with the electrode array substrate, providing a robust foundation for the interface. On top of this layer, an adhesive and antiswelling hydrogel contacts the brain tissue and helps maintain intimate contact with the cortical surface (Fig. 1B). The two layers are connected through a reversible network formed by ferric ions and poly(acrylic acid) (PAA). This network can be strengthened by treating the interface with an Fe3+/citrate solution and selectively disassembled using ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid disodium salt (EDTA) solution (Fig. 1C). EDTA competitively binds Fe3+ ions with higher affinity, disrupting the coordination bonds at the interface, thereby effectively weakening the interfacial bonding between the adhesive and transition layers. The tissue-contacting adhesive layer can therefore be removed from the brain surface without leaving residues and replaced with a fresh one when its performance deteriorates during surgery. This solution-triggered reconfiguration strategy enables the electrode array to maintain a stable and reliable interface with the brain throughout prolonged neurosurgical procedures.
    The tissue-adhesive layer is designed with cationic microspheres, Alg-DA, and PAA-NHS chains. The quaternary ammonium groups on the microspheres form electrostatic interactions with brain tissue, while PAA-NHS and Alg-DA within the hydrogel network provide additional chemical adhesion (Fig. 1D). This gives threefold stronger adhesion on pig brain compared to 3M tapes, while still leaving room for improvement relative to state-of-the-art tissue adhesives (13–16). The cationic microspheres also enhance the mechanical stability of the hydrogel by increasing physical crosslinking and polymer entanglement through electrostatic interactions and hydrogen bonding, which greatly reduces swelling from long-term immersion in biofluid. These multiple dynamic interactions within the network also result in low hysteresis and minimal energy dissipation, helping maintain stable performance during operation.

    Writing in PNAS, Yang et al. report a soft electrode array with reconfigurable hydrogel interfaces enabled by a solution-triggered reconfiguration strategy.
    At the device level, this reconfigurable dual-layer hydrogel is integrated with a PEDOT:PSS-based electrode array, which exhibits a low impedance at 1 kHz, together with higher charge injection and charge storage capacities than commercial electrodes. The dual-layer hydrogel (DH) electrodes were applied to record the electrocorticogram (ECoG) from multiple locations on the brain cortex surface in rabbits, by repeatedly repositioning the electrode array. At the initial placement location on the brain surface, the recorded signals from the DH electrodes showed higher quality than those obtained with commercial electrodes, due to the improved conformability with the brain surface. After 10 repeated repositionings on the cortex surface to different locations, which led to some decline in the adhesion properties, the tissue-adhesive hydrogel interface could be replaced by a new adhesive layer, allowing the device to consistently collect high-quality electrical signals (Fig. 1E). Using this electrode array, the authors were able to capture distinct neural waveform features and evaluate neural conduction pathways by comparing signal amplitudes across different brain regions, enabling the detection of potential neural injury. In contrast, a nonreconfigurable control—an acrylamide-based hydrogel (AH) electrode array—initially provided good contact but showed signal deterioration after several repositioning cycles because of the hydrogel contamination.
    This work demonstrates a materials-level advance in electrode–tissue interfaces, introducing a reconfigurable, high-performance hydrogel interface that can undergo repeated disassembly and replacement. This capability enables the soft electrode array to maintain sustained, high-fidelity signal acquisition and supports accurate assessment of brain activity during neurosurgery, thereby improving surgical safety. Looking ahead, several challenges remain before such systems can be translated into practical biomedical platforms. At the materials level, improving the long-term stability of hydrogel adhesion will be important for maintaining reliable contact with tissue during extended use. From an engineering perspective, integration with high-density electrode arrays may require further reducing device thickness while preserving strong adhesion, so that the spatial resolution of signal recording is not compromised. In addition, extending the reconfigurable hydrogel strategy to other sensing modalities, such as chemical sensors, could broaden its applications, which requires the hydrogel layer to have efficient molecular diffusion while maintaining stable device performance. Addressing these challenges could advance soft neural interfaces for more reliable intraoperative brain monitoring and safer neurosurgical procedures, while opening new opportunities for bioelectronic technologies in healthcare.
